item.title: Autoimmunity and the Good Girls
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Autoimmunity and the Good Girls

How “good girl” roles may be igniting an epidemic of autoimmunity.

Posted May 26, 2026

Key points
  • I have studied my own health and the health of 1000 autoimmune-diagnosed women and the evidence is clear.
  • Self-silencing is making us sick and over-giving is keeping us that way.
  • Abandoning our own wants and needs for a lifetime can create an immune system in identity crisis.
  • I wanted to prove that empowerment may be the missing modality in women's health, so I funded it myself.

“Tell everyone about your book!” my producer, Fred, nudged me as we began a two- hour drive toward Telluride, Colorado, for a documentary shoot the next day.

“It’s okay,” I said. “Everyone’s tired! Long day of filming today.” Read: I’m the one who’s completely talked out, and I just want to doze up here in the front passenger seat.

“No way are you getting out of this!” shouted Jon, my thirty-five-year-old cinematographer.

“Agreed,” said Katrine, my friend and executive producer of the film project.

“You direct and write?” asked Darren, our confused driver.

I shared about how I had been diagnosed with shingles at eight, breast tumors began at 22, an autoimmune condition at 30, and melanoma, active Epstein-Barr, ovarian cysts, heavy metal poisoning, and more between the ages of 42 and 44.

“God, I’m so sorry,” they chorused one by one.

“Wait, what is an autoimmune?” asked Jon.

I shared the CDC definition, essentially, the immunity war the body wages against itself. I shared that there are more than a hundred autoimmune diseases on record, without a single cure for any, with women receiving 80 percent of the diagnoses.

I told them I had always found it fascinating that the majority of my friends had also been diagnosed with an autoimmune disease, and that all of them happened to be either the oldest or the only daughter in their family, as I was. I knew I wanted to explore more, but the birth order observation had been just a hunch. And not being a doctor or a scientist myself, I wanted to stay within my curious documentarian’s lane.

Why, I kept wondering, were all of my friends who grew up too fast, taking care of others more than we took care of ourselves, so sick?

In 2018, I decided to do a poll among 300 women who had an autoimmune disease in our Women Rising social networks to see if the question resonated outside of my personal circle. When the results came in, I was floored: nearly 70 percent of respondents were either the oldest or only daughter.

I knew from my own life that being the eldest daughter made me feel more responsible than the younger daughters I knew. I grew up not wanting to be trouble, or noisy, or needy because I felt punished by the results. I knew that feeling like a disappointment was so traumatizing that I would do self-sacrificing behavioral gymnastics to avoid it.

Dr. Jeffrey Rediger asserts in his book Cured: The Life-Changing Science of Spontaneous Healing, “There is a powerful link between our very identities and our immune systems. Perhaps what ultimately determines the health of the ‘soil’ of your body is how well you know who you really are at the most authentic level— beneath appearances, ‘shoulds,’ perceived expectations, and all the masks and roles that you assume for yourself and the world.”

As a documentary filmmaker, I knew I would need to prove out my theories of birth order and disempowerment at scale before anyone would listen. So I funded it myself.

Autoimmunity and the Good Girls became the first sociological survey exploring the intersection of empowerment and autoimmunity in American women. The survey was fielded by the independent research firm PROOF Insights in November 2023 to 1,000 women who had received at least one autoimmune disease diagnosis.

The results led me to the same conclusion as the instinct that spurred my self-exploration: 63 percent of women with autoimmune diseases said they were either the oldest or the only daughter.

Autoimmunity means our bodies cannot recognize or distinguish healthy cells from unhealthy cells. In other words, our immune systems are having an identity crisis.

But why should my own immune system know who it is and how to recognize itself? I have never known who I truly am or how to recognize myself. I never taught myself how to see myself or how to protect myself, only to abandon myself. Just like so many of us.

In my research for my book Autoimmunity and The Good Girls: How Permission to Put Ourselves First Has the Power to Keep Us Well, I interviewed Sharon, age thirty-five, eldest daughter and autoimmune-diagnosed executive turned Certified Nutrition Specialist (CNS) with a Master's in Human Clinical Nutrition for women with Hashimoto’s. She reflected in our interview, “As an eldest daughter and a caretaker for our parents and younger siblings, you want to grow up just being a normal child. But then parents and other authorities put all of these responsibilities on you.” When I asked Sharon about her own authenticity journey and who she is, who her truest self is after being raised as the consummate “good girl,” she confessed, “If I’m going to be honest, it might be no one. And that feels sad to me to say, but it’s just the truth.”

It is hard not to see that the conditioning of little girls to deprioritize themselves, to neglect themselves, to ignore their own needs, may be yielding an adult immune system that has simply followed directions to do the same.

Adapted from Autoimmunity And The Good Girls: How Permission to Put Ourselves First Has the Power to Keep Us Well (c) 2026 by Sara Hirsh Bordo. Used with permission of the publisher, HarperOne. All rights reserved.

item.title: The Architecture of Healing: Neuroplastogens Explained
item.description:
Neuroplasticity

The Architecture of Healing: Neuroplastogens Explained

The emerging shift toward brain plasticity in mental health.

Posted May 26, 2026

Key points
  • Researchers are studying neuroplasticity as a driver of new mental health treatments.
  • Neuroplastogens aim to promote brain plasticity without hallucinogenic effects.
  • Non-hallucinogenic treatments may improve mental health care accessibility and scalability.
  • Brain plasticity research is reshaping how psychiatry approaches mental health disorders.

Over the past decade, psychedelic medicine has moved from the margins of psychiatric research into mainstream scientific and public discussion. Much of this attention has centered on compounds such as psilocybin, MDMA, ketamine, and related substances that have demonstrated therapeutic potential across conditions including depression, PTSD, anxiety, and addiction.

While discussions often focus on the compounds themselves, an increasingly important area of interest involves the underlying mechanism many researchers believe may contribute to their effects: neuroplasticity.

Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s ability to reorganize, form new neural connections, and adapt in response to experience. In a previous article, I explored how psychedelic compounds may temporarily increase this adaptive capacity, potentially allowing entrenched behavioral and cognitive patterns to become more flexible.

This growing focus on adaptive brain change has contributed to the emergence of a new category of compounds commonly referred to as neuroplastogens. Broadly defined, neuroplastogens are substances designed to promote neuroplasticity and synaptic adaptation, potentially creating conditions that support behavioral and emotional change.

Importantly, some neuroplastogens are being developed specifically to preserve therapeutic effects while minimizing or avoiding hallucinogenic experiences.

Why Non-Hallucinogenic Approaches Matter

Although psychedelic-assisted therapy has generated promising clinical data, the treatment model itself presents several practical challenges. Many current protocols require prolonged monitored sessions, specialized therapeutic support, extensive preparation and integration, and highly controlled clinical environments.

These infrastructure demands may limit scalability, particularly within public health systems already facing resource constraints.

In addition, not all patients are comfortable pursuing treatments that involve intense alterations in consciousness. For certain populations, including individuals with addiction disorders or complex psychiatric histories, hallucinogenic experiences may introduce additional barriers related to safety, accessibility, or treatment acceptance. As a result, researchers and biotechnology companies are increasingly exploring whether neuroplasticity-related benefits can be achieved through non-hallucinogenic approaches.

The objective is not necessarily to replace psychotherapy or psychedelic-assisted treatment models altogether. Rather, the field is beginning to examine whether alternative neuroplasticity-focused interventions may support additional treatment frameworks that are more practical, scalable, and accessible across broader patient populations.

This distinction may become particularly important in addiction treatment, where affordability, clinical capacity, and treatment adherence remain persistent challenges.

A Rapidly Expanding Scientific Field

Interest in neuroplastogens is expanding rapidly across neuroscience, psychiatry, and biotechnology. Several companies are helping shape the neuroplasticity-focused therapeutic field, including Delix Therapeutics, Gilgamesh Pharmaceuticals, and Atai Beckley.

Approaches vary considerably across the sector. Some companies are modifying known psychedelic compounds in an effort to separate neuroplastic effects from hallucinogenic properties. Others are developing entirely novel molecules or exploring alternative delivery systems and treatment protocols designed to improve safety, tolerability, and scalability.

Despite these differences, the broader objective remains relatively consistent: identifying ways to promote adaptive brain change while creating treatment models that can realistically function within large healthcare systems.

This shift reflects a broader evolution in psychiatric research. Increasingly, researchers are exploring whether mental health interventions can move beyond symptom suppression alone and instead support the restoration of more flexible and adaptive neural functioning.

How Neuroplastogens May Influence the Brain

Although the science remains early-stage, many neuroplastogens are believed to interact with serotonin signaling pathways and downstream molecular systems associated with synaptic growth and neuroplasticity. Researchers are investigating whether these compounds may transiently alter the brain’s capacity for adaptation and learning, potentially supporting greater responsiveness to therapeutic interventions.

Several neuroscience mechanisms are frequently discussed in this context: Synaptogenesis refers to the formation of new connections between neurons, while dendritic growth involves increased branching and complexity within neural communication networks. Together, these processes are believed to contribute to the brain’s ability to adapt and reorganize in response to new experiences.

Although much remains under investigation, researchers increasingly view neuroplasticity as a potentially important component in the treatment of disorders characterized by rigid or repetitive behavioral patterns, including substance use disorders.

MEAI and Addiction Research

One compound attracting attention within this emerging category is MEAI, a non-hallucinogenic molecule being developed by Clearmind Medicine (where the author serves as Chief Executive Officer) as a potential treatment for Alcohol Use Disorder.

Early-stage research is exploring whether MEAI may influence reward and reinforcement pathways associated with harmful drinking behaviors. MEAI is being studied for its potential ability to support behavioral change without inducing a hallucinogenic experience.

Clearmind Medicine is investigating MEAI as part of a broader effort to understand whether neuroplasticity-related mechanisms can be leveraged in the treatment of addiction. Within this framework, the company is also exploring whether such approaches could eventually support treatment models that do not rely on prolonged, highly supervised psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy sessions.

Psychotherapy may still play an important complementary role within these frameworks. However, reducing dependence on intensive monitoring and highly specialized infrastructure could potentially improve affordability, accessibility, and scalability if such approaches ultimately demonstrate clinical efficacy.

Scientific Responsibility and the Road Ahead

Despite growing enthusiasm surrounding neuroplastogens, the field remains at an early stage of scientific and clinical development. Many important questions still require rigorous validation, including long-term safety, durability of therapeutic outcomes, optimal dosing strategies, and appropriate treatment settings. Controlled clinical trials, regulatory oversight, and evidence-based implementation will remain essential as research progresses.

At present, neuroplastogens should not be viewed as standalone solutions or universal treatments. Mental health disorders are biologically and psychologically complex, and no single intervention is likely to address the full range of patient needs.

Nevertheless, the growing focus on neuroplasticity reflects an important shift within psychiatric research. Rather than concentrating exclusively on symptom management, researchers are increasingly examining how to support more adaptive neural functioning.

As the field continues to evolve, the future of mental health treatment may increasingly center on helping the brain regain its ability to change itself.

item.title: Best-Practice Support After a Suicide
item.description:
Suicide

Best-Practice Support After a Suicide

The critical difference between suicide prevention and postvention.

Posted May 26, 2026

Key points
  • Most people nowadays are familiar with suicide prevention. Far fewer have heard the term "postvention."
  • After a suicide, organizations often rush to deliver suicide prevention training with the best of intentions.
  • Effective postvention fosters trust, reduces isolation, and strengthens prevention culture.

Most people nowadays are familiar with suicide prevention. Far fewer have heard the term "postvention." Postvention is a specialized area of expertise that is distinct from suicide prevention and a part of the work of suicide prevention at the same time.

In other words, while suicide prevention and suicide postvention are not the same thing, the most effective postvention may be one of the most powerful forms of prevention.

The distinction matters because organizations, families, schools, healthcare systems, military units, and workplaces often respond to suicide loss in ways that unintentionally increase distress instead of reducing it.

Prevention is the work we do before a personal crisis results in a death. It is proactive and ongoing. Strong suicide prevention cultures normalize help-seeking, reduce stigma, strengthen trust, and create systems where people are more likely to speak honestly before hopelessness hardens into despair.

Healthy prevention efforts typically include:

  • Early recognition of behavioral changes and distress
  • Trusted, confidential access to support
  • Leaders who model humanity and openness
  • Strong peer relationships and social connection
  • Wellness woven into daily culture rather than isolated as a standalone program

In practice, prevention is what communities and organizations do every day to reduce the likelihood that someone reaches the point of suicide.

Postvention is different.

Postvention is the structured, compassionate response after a suicide death. It focuses on stabilizing those impacted by the loss, reducing the risk of further harm, and helping people move through grief without becoming isolated inside it.

Importantly, suicide loss survivors are not limited to biological family members. Coworkers, classmates, teammates, close friends, fellow service members, clinicians, or first responders may experience grief just as intensely.

Among other things, postvention includes:

  • Immediate emotional stabilization and support
  • Trauma-informed communication
  • Dignified death notifications and leadership messaging
  • Ongoing peer and psychological support
  • Coordinated efforts to reduce isolation and fear

The problem is that many organizations instinctively respond to suicide loss with conventional prevention training. The intention is understandable: Leaders want to act quickly. But timing and psychological context matter.

Someone grieving a suicide is often already asking themselves:

  • Why didn’t I see the signs?
  • Why didn’t they trust me enough to tell me?
  • Who else might I lose?

Flooding survivors with warning-sign education immediately after a loss can unintentionally intensify guilt, shame, hypervigilance, and traumatic stress. Compulsory training delivered too early may feel less like support and more like a liability-driven response.

What grieving people need first is not education. They need connection, stabilization, and compassionate leadership.

This is where postvention becomes prevention.

Research shows that people exposed to suicide loss are themselves at heightened risk for depression, traumatic stress, and suicidal thoughts. The period after a suicide death is therefore a psychologically vulnerable window in which leadership and culture matter enormously.

People remember how leaders respond after tragedy. They remember whether leadership showed up or disappeared. They remember whether communication felt human or scripted. Silence itself can become a rupture in trust.

By contrast, effective postvention sends a deeply protective message: You matter here. We will not abandon each other in pain.

That message reduces isolation, strengthens psychological safety, and increases trust in support systems—all of which are protective against suicide risk.

Postvention is both reactive and proactive by its nature. It is reactive because, by definition, postvention strategies are engaged in the aftermath of a death by suicide. However, it must also be proactive because passive resource offering (“we have counselors here to support—reach out if you need help”) often fails to meet the needs of people who are not internally organized enough to seek help during what is a devastating tsunami of grief and trauma. Passive resource offering also fails those who must overcome substantial cultural barriers to seeking support.

Strong postvention also shapes culture over time. It deepens trust in leadership, normalizes help-seeking, strengthens peer connection, and often transforms survivors into powerful allies in future prevention efforts.

In this sense, postvention is not the opposite of prevention. It is prevention after impact.

And in the aftermath of suicide, the question people are asking internally is not simply whether help exists. It is whether anyone will truly stand beside them in their grief.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
